The correlation between the baseline proportion of intra-tumoral immune cell subtypes and the tumor regression ratio (TRR) following anti-PD-1 therapy in 22 CRC patients is predominantly positive for T-cell subtypes.

Specifically, among 91 cell subtypes tested, three showed nominally significant positive correlations with TRR (Pearson p < 0.05, none surviving FDR correction):

1. c13_CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9 (activated regulatory T cells): r = +0.505, p = 0.017
2. c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN (exhausted CD8+ T cells): r = +0.474, p = 0.026
3. c68_Endo_FABP5 (endothelial cells): r = +0.450, p = 0.036

All three significant correlations are positive. Across all 91 subtypes, 40 (44%) showed positive correlations and 51 (56%) showed negative correlations with TRR, but the T-cell-enriched subtypes consistently trended positive.

This implies that higher baseline infiltration of activated T cells — particularly exhausted CD8+ T cells (LAYN+) and activated regulatory T cells (TNFRSF9+) — is associated with greater tumor regression after anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade. This supports the model that a pre-existing T-cell-inflamed tumor microenvironment is necessary for immunotherapy response, consistent with published literature on checkpoint blockade mechanisms (Tumeh et al., 2014, Nature; Sade-Feldman et al., 2018, Cell).

**Biological implication:** Higher baseline infiltration of activated/exhausted T cells in the tumor microenvironment is associated with greater tumor regression, supporting the model that pre-existing T cell immunity is necessary for anti-PD-1 response.
